meta.heading: Round 3: technical looks and four kinds of map
meta.intro: Paper is out; technical is in. C's sliding sheets stay in every direction. Round 2 is in the Archive with my replies. Notes to Claude can now take pictures: paste screenshots of apps you like and I'll work from them.

r3-look.title: Four technical looks. Every one keeps C's sliding sheets
body: Each one is built from tools people who work with computers already know. Click **Open the project** on each one to see the sheet slide in, then go back.
They're shown dark because that's how these tools usually look. Every direction gets a matching light version, and your manual light/dark switch is already decided.

figures.caption: **D · Workbench.** Like VS Code: icon bar, a section list, tabs, and a status bar at the bottom that always shows today's hours, the week and anything overdue.
**E · Blueprint.** An engineering drawing: grid paper, hours drawn as dimension lines, and a title block in the corner with the date and totals.
**F · Ops console.** Like a monitoring dashboard: number tiles, today as a bar against an 8-hour day, and recurring work shown as health checks with status lights.
**G · Keyboard-first.** Like Linear or Raycast: calm rows, "Needs attention" at the top, ticket numbers in monospace, and a keyboard shortcut for every section.

bullets: Where these come from: **VS Code** (D), CAD and technical drawings (E), **Grafana** and network monitoring tools (F), and **Linear**, **Raycast** and **Superhuman** (G). People with ADHD often like the last group because one screen shows what needs you, and the keyboard gets you anywhere without hunting.
Mixing is fine. For example, G's rows with D's status bar, or F's health lights for recurring work inside any of them.

options.label: G, with D's status bar and F's health lights for recurring work
options.why: Calm, scannable rows; totals always in view at the bottom; recurring work you can read at a glance.
Send me screenshots of apps you like in Notes to Claude.

questions.legend: What do you like or dislike in any of them? (optional)
questions.placeholder: e.g. E's title block is fun, F feels too busy

r3-look.pick: G, with D's status bar and F's health lights.

r3-map.title: Four ways to draw the notes map
body: Same sample notes, tasks and projects, drawn four ways. Click any item to trace what it connects to. These are drawn dark to sit with the technical looks.

Understood about the list: it's just the main pages, so the map doesn't need a list mode of its own. Links are made automatically from shared tickets, projects and words, as you picked; you can delete a wrong one.

figures.caption: **1 · Node editor.** Like Node-RED or Blender's node view: typed boxes with a coloured header, wires between ports, P1–P3 priority on each box.
**2 · Swimlanes.** A process diagram: one lane per project, time runs left to right, arrows show what led to what.
**3 · Metro map.** Each project is a line; notes and tasks are stops in date order. Dotted lines are links between projects.
**4 · Timeline.** Dates along the middle; notes above, tasks below, coloured by project.

questions.legend: Which is closest to what you pictured?

options.why: Reads as a process diagram, fits the technical looks, and stays readable as it grows.
Describe it below or send a sketch or screenshot in Notes to Claude.

questions.legend: Anything about what you pictured that none of these show? (optional)
questions.placeholder: e.g. I want to drag notes onto each other to link them

r3-map.pick: 1, the node editor. It could also switch to 2 for a single project, since lanes read well for one stream of work.

r3-attach.title: Notes to Claude can now carry pictures
body: In **Notes to Claude**, paste a screenshot straight into the text box, or use **Attach pictures**. Up to 8 per note. They're stored with this page, so I can open them in any session.
Good uses: an app whose look you like, a photo of a sketch on paper, or a screenshot of a muddle you want Shiftbook to fix.
